newsitem.title: USA: Ford continues to focus on European cost cutting.
newsitem.headline: Ford continues to focus on European cost cutting.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. executives said Tuesday they will try to avoid closing plants as the automaker works to stem the flow of red ink from its European operations.

"There's no guarantees, but that's clearly something we don't want to do," Ford Automotive President Jacques Nasser said in an interview. "We prefer to use the facilities and the resources we've got."
Nasser, who spoke at the North American International Auto Show here, said the company wass not prepared to talk publicly about how it planned to streamline its money-losing European operations.

Nasser said Ford was talking with unions representing workers at its Halewood plant in Britain about ways to reduce costs at the facility. The plant is one of three that makes the Escort. He declined to discuss the specifics of the talks.

"Clearly, our wish is to utilize the existing facilities we have in the UK and to have a good employment career future for our employees there. But we have to work together because, in the end, no one owes us living," he said.

Ford Chairman Alex Trotman has previously said the company can probably serve its European market needs with less capacity. On Tuesday, Trotman told reporters the automaker was focusing on driving down European costs in all areas, including fixed costs, capacity utilization, material costs and inventory.
"It's a major priority for us, and it's on all cost elements," he said.
Ford's European operations, which are experiencing bruising price competition and several new model launches, lost $420 million in the third quarter.
Trotman declined to comment on fourth-quarter results, which have not yet been released, but said first-quarter numbers will show an improvement.
"I expect to be profitable in Europe in 1997," he said.
In Brazil, another money-losing area for Ford, the company continues to gain market share, Trotman said, but will still probably post a loss in 1997.
Ford's share of the Brazilian market fell by half when it was part of the Autolatina joint venture with Volkswagen AG, said Trotman. That venture has been disbanded.

Last year, Ford introduced a new Fiesta in Brazil, but ran into higher-than-expected launch costs that led to losses in the third quarter. Ford plans to introduce its new small car, the Ka, in Brazil next month.

Nasser said he did not believe Ford would need to cut more salaried positions in 1997. Last year, the automaker offered early retirement buyouts designed to reduce its staff by 4,000 in the United States, Europe, and Latin America.
"We're not planning to do that (this year)," he said. "It's largely behind us now both in the U.S. and in Europe."
Many of those let go in 1996 were contract, supplemental and outside agency workers, Nasser said.
